title: Human Factors: Automation, Trust and Reliance
subtitle: The classic literature that HAI builds on
overview: Classic human factors research on how pilots, operators and clinicians over-rely and under-rely on automation: ironies and levels of automation, trust, judgment biases, automation bias, algorithm aversion, and social responses to computers. Modern HAI studies borrow these concepts; ask how each applies to LLM assistants.

modules.title: Ironies and levels of automation
modules.goal: Explain why automating a task can make the human's remaining job harder, and describe automation in terms of stages and levels.
modules.guide: Start with Bainbridge's short paper; it fits AI assistants closely. Parasuraman and Riley name ways automation is used badly. Parasuraman, Sheridan and Wickens classify automation by stage and level. Endsley is optional. Key terms: operator (the person using the system); vigilance (sustained attention to rare events); misuse (over-relying); disuse (ignoring helpful automation); level of automation (how much the machine does); situation awareness (knowing what's happening, what it means, what's next).

resources.title: Ironies of automation
resources.why: Explains why automation changes the human's job, often for the worse, rather than removing human error.
resources.focus: The paper is short. Note each 'irony' and the proposed remedies.

resources.title: Humans and Automation: Use, Misuse, Disuse, Abuse
resources.why: Defines four ways people relate to automation; 'misuse' (over-reliance) and 'disuse' (under-reliance) are standard HAI terms.
resources.focus: The four category definitions, the trust and false-alarm sections, and the recommendations.

resources.title: A model for types and levels of human interaction with automation
resources.authors: Raja Parasuraman, Thomas B. Sheridan, Christopher D. Wickens
resources.venue: IEEE Transactions on Systems, Man, and Cybernetics, Part A
resources.why: The standard four-stage, levels-of-automation framework, often used to classify AI decision aids.
resources.focus: The four-stage figure, the levels table, and evaluation criteria (workload, situation awareness, complacency, skill degradation).

resources.title: Toward a Theory of Situation Awareness in Dynamic Systems
resources.why: Situation awareness is the concept behind worries that AI assistance leaves users 'out of the loop'.
resources.focus: The definition and the three levels of situation awareness; skim the rest.

quiz.q: What is the central irony Bainbridge describes?
choices: Automation always increases the operator's workload during normal operation
Automation takes over the routine work but leaves the operator to monitor it and to step in during rare, difficult situations, for which their skills have faded
Operators refuse to use automation that works well
Automated systems never fail, so operators become bored
quiz.explain: Bainbridge points out that the designer automates what is easy to automate, leaving the human the hardest part (handling abnormal events) while removing the practice that keeps their skills sharp.

quiz.q: What does Bainbridge say about asking humans to monitor a highly reliable automated system?
choices: Humans are excellent monitors if paid well
Monitoring is the easiest task to give a person
People are poor at sustaining attention for long periods on something that rarely goes wrong
Monitoring should be done only by the system's designers
quiz.explain: Bainbridge draws on vigilance research: humans cannot keep effective watch for very long on a system where abnormal events are rare. The same problem arises when users are asked to 'check the AI's output'.

quiz.q: A clinician learns to ignore a sepsis alarm that fires many times a day, mostly falsely, and then misses a real case. In Parasuraman and Riley's terms, this is:
choices: Disuse
Misuse
Abuse
Appropriate use
quiz.explain: Disuse is the neglect or underuse of automation; Parasuraman and Riley identify frequent false alarms as a common cause. Misuse would be the opposite: over-relying on it.

quiz.q: Parasuraman and Riley define 'automation abuse' as:
choices: Users deliberately breaking automated systems
Users trusting automation too much
Automation that has been hacked
Designers and managers automating functions without regard for the consequences for human performance
quiz.explain: Abuse is a design and management failure: the operator's role becomes whatever is left over after automation, which can in turn promote misuse and disuse.

quiz.q: Why do Parasuraman and Riley say alarms often fire falsely?
choices: Sensors are always cheap and noisy
Thresholds are set without considering the base rate of the condition, so when the condition is rare, most alarms are false even for a sensitive detector
Operators reset them too often
Alarms are tested only in simulators
quiz.explain: The abstract notes that false alarms commonly arise because the base rate of the event is ignored when trading off false alarms against misses.

quiz.q: In Parasuraman, Sheridan and Wickens's four-stage model, a lane-keeping system that physically steers the car automates which stage?
choices: Information acquisition
Information analysis
Decision and action selection
Action implementation
quiz.explain: The four stages are information acquisition, information analysis, decision and action selection, and action implementation. Executing the steering itself is action implementation.

quiz.q: What is a key point of the Parasuraman, Sheridan and Wickens model?
choices: A system can have different levels of automation at each of the four stages, so it is not simply 'high' or 'low' automation
Full automation is always the goal
Levels of automation apply only to aviation
Only the decision stage should ever be automated
quiz.explain: The authors describe automation as a profile across stages, and recommend choosing levels by evaluating human performance consequences such as workload, situation awareness, complacency and skill degradation.

modules.exercise: Pick an AI coding assistant or LLM agent you know. Classify its functions using Parasuraman, Sheridan and Wickens's four stages and estimate a level of automation for each. Then name one of Bainbridge's ironies likely to affect its users and propose a measure that would detect it in a study that follows users over several months.

modules.title: Trust in automation and AI
modules.goal: Define trust, distinguish it from reliance, and explain what 'calibrated' or 'warranted' trust means.
modules.guide: Read Lee and See first, slowly. Mayer, Davis and Schoorman give the interpersonal model Lee and See adapt; Hoff and Bashir organize later findings into layers; Jacovi et al. apply them to AI. Key terms: trust (an attitude that an agent will help amid uncertainty and vulnerability); reliance (actually depending on it); calibration (trust matching real capability); trustworthiness (system properties that justify trust); warranted trust (trust caused by actual trustworthiness).

resources.title: Trust in Automation: Designing for Appropriate Reliance
resources.authors: John D. Lee, Katrina A. See
resources.why: The most cited paper on trust in automation; source of 'appropriate reliance' and 'trust calibration'.
resources.focus: Trust definition; the calibration, resolution and specificity figure; bases of trust (performance, process, purpose); design recommendations.

resources.title: An Integrative Model of Organizational Trust
resources.authors: Roger C. Mayer, James H. Davis, F. David Schoorman
resources.why: The ability-benevolence-integrity trust model that much trust-in-AI research adapts.
resources.focus: Trust definition, the three trustworthiness factors, and the trustor's propensity.

resources.title: Trust in Automation: Integrating Empirical Evidence on Factors That Influence Trust
resources.why: A systematic review distilling a decade of experiments into a three-layer model, useful for choosing study variables.
resources.focus: The three-layer model and its figure, and the design recommendations.

resources.title: Formalizing Trust in Artificial Intelligence: Prerequisites, Causes and Goals of Human Trust in AI
resources.authors: Alon Jacovi, Ana Marasović, Tim Miller, Yoav Goldberg
resources.why: Defines trust in AI, introducing 'contractual' and 'warranted' trust, terms common in XAI and HAI evaluation.
resources.focus: Prerequisites of trust, contractual trust, warranted versus unwarranted trust, and intrinsic versus extrinsic causes.

quiz.q: How do Lee and See define trust?
choices: The percentage of time a person uses automation
The attitude that an agent will help achieve an individual's goals in a situation characterized by uncertainty and vulnerability
A belief that a machine is always correct
A measure of a system's reliability
quiz.explain: Lee and See define trust as an attitude, not a behavior and not a system property. This lets them separate trust from reliance, which is what people actually do.

quiz.q: In Lee and See's framework, what does good 'calibration' mean?
choices: The user's trust matches the automation's actual capabilities
Trust is as high as possible
The automation adjusts its outputs to the user's mood
The user tests the system once before use
quiz.explain: Calibration is the correspondence between trust and capability. Overtrust leads to misuse and distrust to disuse, using Parasuraman and Riley's terms.

quiz.q: Why do Lee and See insist on separating trust from reliance?
choices: They are always identical in experiments
Reliance cannot be measured
Trust guides reliance, but other factors such as workload, time pressure and self-confidence also affect whether people rely on automation
Reliance only applies to humans, not machines
quiz.explain: A person may distrust a system yet rely on it because they are overloaded, or trust it yet act manually. HAI studies therefore measure behavioral reliance separately from self-reported trust.

quiz.q: Mayer, Davis and Schoorman identify three factors of trustworthiness. Which set is it?
choices: Speed, accuracy, cost
Familiarity, liking, similarity
Transparency, reliability, safety
Ability, benevolence, integrity
quiz.explain: Ability (competence in the domain), benevolence (wanting to do good for the trustor) and integrity (adhering to acceptable principles). Lee and See map these onto performance, purpose and process.

quiz.q: In Hoff and Bashir's model, a user trusts the same AI tool less when the decision is high-stakes. Which layer of trust is this?
choices: Dispositional trust
Situational trust
Learned trust
Contractual trust
quiz.explain: Hoff and Bashir separate dispositional trust (the person's general tendency), situational trust (depends on the context, such as risk and workload) and learned trust (built from experience with the system).

quiz.q: According to Jacovi et al., when is a user's trust in an AI 'warranted'?
choices: When the user reports high trust on a questionnaire
When the AI has been approved by a regulator
When the trust is caused by the AI actually being trustworthy with respect to the relevant contract
Whenever the AI is accurate on average
quiz.explain: Jacovi et al. define warranted trust by its cause: trust that arises from the model's real trustworthiness, rather than from irrelevant cues like a confident tone.

quiz.q: Jacovi et al. name two prerequisites for trust in AI. What are they?
choices: The user is vulnerable to the AI's actions, and the user can anticipate the impact of the AI's decisions
The AI is open source, and the user is an expert
The AI explains itself, and the user agrees
The user has used the AI before, and it never erred
quiz.explain: The abstract states the model rests on the user's vulnerability and the ability to anticipate the impact of the model's decisions, echoing the vulnerability in Mayer et al.'s and Lee and See's definitions.

modules.exercise: Design a study that measures appropriate reliance on an AI advisor, not just self-reported trust. Specify the task, how you would vary the AI's accuracy across trials, a behavioral reliance measure, and how you would tell whether reliance is calibrated (tracks when the AI is right) rather than just high or low overall.

modules.title: Heuristics, biases and automation bias
modules.goal: Explain the main judgment heuristics, and describe automation bias, its two error types, and what strengthens or weakens it.
modules.guide: Read Tversky and Kahneman (1974), the basis of 'heuristics and biases', then Skitka, Mosier and Burdick's automation bias experiment and Goddard et al.'s review (especially healthcare). Key terms: heuristic (a useful shortcut that causes systematic errors); anchoring (estimates pulled toward an initial number); base rate (how common something is); automation bias (automated cues replacing careful checking); omission error (missing an unflagged problem); commission error (following a wrong recommendation).

resources.title: Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
resources.why: Introduces representativeness, availability and anchoring, the vocabulary for how AI advice can bias judgment.
resources.focus: Read all three heuristic sections and their examples.

resources.title: Does automation bias decision-making?
resources.authors: Linda J. Skitka, Kathleen L. Mosier, Mark Burdick
resources.why: The classic experiment showing that a reliable but imperfect decision aid produces new kinds of errors.
resources.focus: Introduction (definitions of omission and commission errors), method and main results.

resources.title: Automation bias: a systematic review of frequency, effect mediators, and mitigators
resources.authors: Kate Goddard, Abdul Roudsari, Jeremy C. Wyatt
resources.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association
resources.why: Summarizes when automation bias is stronger or weaker and what reduces it, directly relevant to clinical AI.
resources.focus: Abstract, the tables of mediators and mitigators, and the discussion.

quiz.q: Which three heuristics do Tversky and Kahneman describe?
choices: Framing, loss aversion and endowment
Representativeness, availability, and adjustment and anchoring
Confirmation, hindsight and overconfidence
Recognition, fluency and affect
quiz.explain: The 1974 paper is organized around these three heuristics. Loss aversion and framing come from Kahneman and Tversky's later work.

quiz.q: In Tversky and Kahneman's experiment, a spun wheel produced a random number and people then estimated the percentage of African countries in the UN. Their estimates moved toward the random number. Which heuristic does this show?
choices: Availability
Representativeness
Anchoring
Base-rate neglect
quiz.explain: Even an obviously arbitrary starting value acted as an anchor that people adjusted from insufficiently. An AI's suggestion shown before a person forms their own judgment can work the same way.

quiz.q: In Skitka et al.'s terms, an automated aid fails to flag an engine problem and the participant misses it, even though other instruments showed it. This is:
choices: An error of omission
An error of commission
Disuse
A false alarm
quiz.explain: Omission errors are failures to notice problems the automation did not point out. Commission errors are following an automated directive that is wrong, despite contrary evidence.

quiz.q: What was the key comparison in Skitka et al. (1999)?
choices: Pilots versus students on the same task
Two different automated aids
Participants with a reliable but imperfect automated aid versus participants without one, on events where the aid failed or was wrong
Paper checklists versus spoken checklists
quiz.explain: Participants with the aid made omission and commission errors, while those without it performed better on exactly those events. Having the aid changed how people monitored.

quiz.q: Goddard et al. list environmental factors that increase automation bias. Which is one?
choices: High workload or time pressure
A well-lit room
Using a desktop instead of a laptop
Having more decision options
quiz.explain: The review names workload, task complexity and time constraints, which put pressure on cognitive resources, alongside user factors such as experience, trust and confidence.

quiz.q: Which mitigation of automation bias is reported in Goddard et al.'s review?
choices: Hiding the system's confidence level
Removing training to avoid priming users
Training and emphasizing users' accountability, plus design choices such as showing updated confidence levels
Always presenting a single firm recommendation
quiz.explain: Goddard et al. list training, user accountability, the position of advice on screen, confidence levels and providing information rather than a recommendation as mitigators.

modules.exercise: Critique: Skitka et al. ran a laboratory flight-simulation task with student participants. List three threats to generalizing their findings to professional pilots or to clinicians using an AI diagnostic tool. Then propose a study design that addresses one of those threats while still allowing you to measure omission and commission errors.

modules.title: Algorithm aversion and appreciation
modules.goal: Explain when people avoid algorithmic advice and when they prefer it, and how expectation-setting and control change acceptance.
modules.guide: Dietvorst et al. 2015 and Logg et al. 2019 seem to conflict; check what participants saw first. Dietvorst et al. 2018 (optional) tests a remedy; Kocielnik et al. study a real system. Key terms: algorithm aversion (avoiding an algorithm after it errs, though it beats humans); algorithm appreciation (more weight on advice labeled algorithmic); weight of advice (shift toward advice, 0 to 1); expectation setting (stating an AI's limits upfront).

resources.title: Algorithm aversion: People erroneously avoid algorithms after seeing them err.
resources.authors: Berkeley J. Dietvorst, Joseph P. Simmons, Cade Massey
resources.why: Coined 'algorithm aversion', one of the most cited findings in human-AI decision making.
resources.focus: Introduction, Study 1's design (four conditions), and the general discussion.

resources.title: Algorithm appreciation: People prefer algorithmic to human judgment
resources.authors: Jennifer M. Logg, Julia A. Minson, Don A. Moore
resources.venue: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
resources.why: The counterpoint to algorithm aversion, with a reusable experimental paradigm (weight of advice).
resources.focus: Introduction, Experiment 1A, Experiments 3 and 4 (where appreciation fades), and the discussion.

resources.title: Overcoming Algorithm Aversion: People Will Use Imperfect Algorithms If They Can (Even Slightly) Modify Them
resources.authors: Berkeley J. Dietvorst, Joseph P. Simmons, Cade Massey
resources.why: Shows that giving people a small amount of control increases their willingness to use an algorithm.
resources.focus: Introduction and Study 2 (sensitivity to how much modification is allowed).

resources.title: Will You Accept an Imperfect AI?
resources.authors: Rafal Kocielnik, Saleema Amershi, Paul N. Bennett
resources.why: Shows an AI's error type, and how users are prepared for it, shape acceptance as much as accuracy.
resources.focus: The Scheduling Assistant setup, the two error-focus versions, and the three expectation-adjustment techniques.

quiz.q: What did Dietvorst et al. (2015) find?
choices: People always prefer algorithms to humans
People are less likely to choose an algorithm after seeing it make errors, even when they have seen it outperform a human forecaster
People cannot tell algorithms and humans apart
Algorithms perform worse than people at forecasting
quiz.explain: Across several studies, seeing the algorithm perform, and therefore err, reduced choosing it, even though it beat the human forecasts. The word 'erroneously' in the title reflects that this choice cost participants money.

quiz.q: Which asymmetry is central to Dietvorst et al.'s explanation of algorithm aversion?
choices: People lose confidence in an algorithm faster than in a human forecaster after seeing the same mistakes
People forgive algorithms faster than humans
People trust algorithms only when they are free
People never see their own mistakes
quiz.explain: The authors argue that people hold algorithms to a different standard and lose confidence in them more quickly after errors than they do in humans.

quiz.q: Logg et al. (2019) found 'algorithm appreciation'. Under which condition did it weaken?
choices: When advice was shown on a phone
When the algorithm was described in detail
When people were paid
When people chose between an algorithm's estimate and their own (rather than another person's), and when participants were experienced forecasters
quiz.explain: Appreciation waned when the comparison was with one's own judgment (Experiment 3) and among professionals with forecasting expertise (Experiment 4), who relied less on the algorithm and were less accurate as a result.

quiz.q: How can Dietvorst et al.'s aversion and Logg et al.'s appreciation both be true?
choices: One of the papers must be fraudulent
Logg et al. used only experts
Aversion appears after people see the algorithm err; Logg et al.'s participants mostly received advice without first watching the algorithm make mistakes
They studied different countries
quiz.explain: The key difference is the evidence participants had. Dietvorst's effect is triggered by observed errors, so it is not a general dislike of algorithms. Logg et al. measured initial reliance on advice.

quiz.q: In Dietvorst et al. (2018), what increased people's use of an imperfect algorithm?
choices: Letting them modify its forecasts, even by a small, restricted amount
Hiding its errors
Describing it as artificial intelligence
Raising the payment for accuracy
quiz.explain: People were much more willing to use the algorithm when they could adjust its output, and this preference held even when allowed adjustments were tiny, suggesting a desire for some control rather than a lot.

quiz.q: Kocielnik et al. built two versions of a meeting-detection assistant with the same 50% accuracy. What differed, and what did it affect?
choices: Their speed; it affected nothing
Their color scheme; it affected trust
Their training data; it affected accuracy
Whether they focused on avoiding false positives or false negatives; this led to very different perceived accuracy and acceptance
quiz.explain: Holding accuracy fixed, the type of error the system avoided changed how users perceived and accepted it. The paper also shows that expectation-adjustment techniques increased acceptance.

modules.exercise: Critique: in Dietvorst et al. (2015), participants who saw the algorithm's track record also earned money for accurate forecasts and, in some conditions, saw their own track record. What explanations other than 'people hold algorithms to a higher standard' could account for the drop in choosing the algorithm? Propose one additional condition that would rule out an alternative you named.

modules.title: Social responses to machines
modules.goal: Explain why people treat computers as social actors, how that differs from believing they're human, and what drives anthropomorphism.
modules.guide: Nass, Steuer and Tauber launched 'Computers Are Social Actors' (CASA): swap a person for a computer in a social psychology finding and test it. Nass and Moon review evidence and argue for mindlessness. Epley, Waytz and Cacioppo theorize when people anthropomorphize; Abercrombie et al. (optional) apply this to dialogue systems. Key terms: mindlessness (automatic response to cues); anthropomorphism (giving non-humans human traits); effectance (the drive to understand and predict surroundings).

resources.title: Computers are social actors
resources.authors: Clifford Nass, Jonathan Steuer, Ellen R. Tauber
resources.why: Founded the CASA paradigm, still the basis of much chatbot research.
resources.focus: The paradigm and the politeness experiment; note participants' own accounts of their behavior.

resources.title: Machines and Mindlessness: Social Responses to Computers
resources.why: Summarizes a decade of CASA studies and explains why 'people think computers are human' is wrong.
resources.focus: The three study sets (social categories, overlearned behaviors, premature cognitive commitments) and the alternative-explanations section.

resources.title: On seeing human: A three-factor theory of anthropomorphism.
resources.authors: Nicholas Epley, Adam Waytz, John T. Cacioppo
resources.why: The standard theory of anthropomorphism, used to predict which users humanize an AI and when.
resources.focus: The introduction and the sections on each of the three factors.

resources.title: Mirages: On Anthropomorphism in Dialogue Systems
resources.authors: Gavin Abercrombie, Amanda Cercas Curry, Tanvi Dinkar, Verena Rieser, Zeerak Talat
resources.why: Applies anthropomorphism research to chatbots, listing design and linguistic cues that make people personify them.

quiz.q: In the CASA politeness study, participants rated a computer's performance. When were their ratings more positive?
choices: When the same computer asked for the evaluation, compared with a different computer or paper
When they rated it on paper
When they were told it was a human
When the room was empty
quiz.explain: People gave kinder evaluations 'to the computer's face', just as they are polite to a person asking about their own performance, even though nobody believed the computer had feelings.

quiz.q: In the CASA studies Nass and Moon review, how did participants' stated beliefs compare with their behavior?
choices: They said they believed computers have feelings, and acted accordingly
They refused to interact with the computers
They said the experimenter told them to be polite
They agreed computers are not human and should not be treated as such, yet still responded to them socially
quiz.explain: Participants endorsed the view that computers are not people, yet behaved socially anyway. This gap between belief and behavior is the heart of the CASA result and the reason Nass and Moon reject conscious anthropomorphism as the explanation.

quiz.q: Nass and Moon explain social responses to computers through 'mindlessness'. Which explanation do they argue against?
choices: That people respond automatically to social cues
That people consciously believe computers are human (anthropomorphism)
That overlearned behaviors are triggered by cues
That people use social categories as shortcuts
quiz.explain: Nass and Moon argue people know computers are not human; they respond mindlessly to cues like voice or language. They reject both anthropomorphism and deliberate social responses as explanations.

quiz.q: In Nass and Moon's review, viewers perceived content from a television labeled as a 'specialist' (for example, a news set) as better. This illustrates:
choices: Gender stereotyping
Reciprocity
Premature cognitive commitment
Ethnic identification
quiz.explain: A label accepted without reflection shaped later judgments. In LLM terms, telling users an assistant is an 'expert' could have a similar effect.

quiz.q: In Epley et al.'s theory, a lonely user is more likely to anthropomorphize a chatbot. Which factor explains this?
choices: Elicited agent knowledge
Effectance motivation
Sociality motivation
Mindlessness
quiz.explain: The three factors are elicited agent knowledge (using knowledge about humans as a template), effectance motivation (the need to understand and predict) and sociality motivation (the need for social connection). Loneliness raises sociality motivation.

quiz.q: According to Epley et al., why might an unpredictable AI system be anthropomorphized more than a predictable one?
choices: Unpredictability raises effectance motivation, so people reach for human-like explanations to make sense of its behavior
Unpredictable systems are always more humanlike in appearance
People ignore unpredictable systems
Unpredictability lowers sociality motivation
quiz.explain: Effectance motivation is the drive to explain and predict an agent. When behavior is hard to predict, treating the agent as having human-like intentions is a ready way to make sense of it.

quiz.q: What do Abercrombie et al. recommend to dialogue system developers?
choices: Make systems as humanlike as possible to build trust
Take care in design, development, release and description, paying attention to the linguistic cues that lead users to personify the system
Stop building dialogue systems
Use only voice interfaces
quiz.explain: Abercrombie et al. argue that anthropomorphism can lead to over-reliance and other harms, and that it is partly driven by design choices developers control.

modules.exercise: Design a CASA-style replication with a modern LLM chatbot: adapt the politeness study (or another Nass and Moon finding) to an open-ended chat. What changes now that the system produces fluent, human-like language? How would you tell a mindless social response apart from a deliberate one, and what control condition would you use?
